doc.title: Howard Mandel interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: The future of Down Beat and where Mandel writes
summary: He discusses Down Beat's missed potential, a coming publisher change, other magazines he writes for and the rise of jazz books.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: And Down Beat’s been around for an awful long time. Is it healthy? A good future for it?

Oh — now you’re going to get me in trouble. I think actually DownBeat has made some changes recently that I’m not really at liberty to talk about but I think they are about to announce a change in the publisher that I think will be good for it. DownBeat is in some ways frustrating. Down Beat could have been Rolling Stone. DownBeat was the music magazine before there were music magazines in this country. DownBeat could have been Spin. It has to do with the — dare I say — narrow ambitions of the publications that did not grow in that way and thrive in that way. Now it’s given birth to Jazz Times and Jazziz. But I don’t think it’s served the music in the way that it might have. I wish it will. I hope it will sometime. And it’s not the only publication — I mean I’ve worked with them since ’74 but I have written for Jazz Times and Jazziz, and really anybody who’d pay me. Swing Journal, The Wire, Witme, which is a Finnish jazz magazine, Bravo from Brazil, Italian jazz magazines, Swiss magazines. There’s a lot of journalism and publication about the music but it’s very scattered and seldom in one place. We are seeing a lot of great jazz writing in book form now, and that’s very unusual. That was not happening twenty years ago. It’s very difficult — I don’t think that the publishers are making a lot of money on most of the jazz biographies and collections, histories that are coming out but they seem to be willing to take a chance on it. I think that’s a good thing.
